transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you—thanks for coming in today. What has been bothering you lately that made you decide to come see me?

I’ve been having these really strong beliefs about things going on around me that other people keep telling me aren’t real, but they still feel completely real to me. It’s been going on for a long time and it’s starting to really stress me out and affect my day-to-day life, so I thought I should get help.

Over the past few months, have you had any long periods when your mood was unusually low or, on the other hand, unusually high or energized, where these mood changes clearly stood out from how you usually feel?

I don’t think I’ve had anything like that that really stands out. I get stressed and worried because of these beliefs, but I haven’t noticed any long stretches of being really down or overly energetic that feel different from my usual self.
How long have you been experiencing these strong beliefs—would you say it’s been less than a month, between one and six months, or more than six months continuously?
It’s definitely been more than six months continuously. I’d say it’s been going on for almost two years now without really letting up.

Apart from these strong beliefs, have you also noticed things like hearing voices that others can’t hear, feeling your thoughts are being interfered with or controlled, or your thoughts getting very jumbled or hard to follow?
No, I don’t hear voices that other people can’t hear. I don’t feel like anyone is controlling my thoughts, and my thinking feels pretty clear to me, not especially jumbled.

Do you ever find yourself questioning whether these beliefs might be mistaken, or are you completely convinced they are true even when they cause problems in your work, relationships, or daily activities?

Most of the time I feel completely sure they’re true, even when people argue with me about them. Very occasionally I’ll wonder for a moment if I might be overreacting, but that doubt doesn’t really last. They’ve caused some tension with family and a few issues at work, but aside from dealing with that, I feel like I function pretty normally.

Can you briefly describe one or two of these strong beliefs and tell me whether people from your family, culture, or close community generally share these ideas, or if they say they seem unusual just for you?

One big one is that I’m being watched and monitored, like there are people or some organization tracking me through my phone and even when I’m out in public, and that a lot of small things around me—like comments on TV or strangers’ conversations—are actually messages directed at me. My family and friends all say these ideas sound unusual and that they don’t see any evidence of it, so it feels like I’m the only one who believes this.

Have you used any drugs or substances (such as cannabis, stimulants like cocaine or meth, hallucinogens, or large amounts of alcohol) around the time these beliefs started or since then, and if so, did they make these experiences stronger or more frequent?

I don’t really use drugs—just an occasional drink socially, maybe a couple of beers on a weekend. I didn’t start or change any substance use around the time these beliefs began, and I haven’t noticed alcohol making them any better or worse.

Over the past couple of years, have you noticed changes like becoming much more withdrawn, losing motivation or interest in things you used to enjoy, or having trouble taking care of daily tasks (like hygiene or work), beyond the stress caused by these beliefs themselves?

Not really beyond what’s directly related to these beliefs. I still go to work, keep up with my responsibilities, and take care of myself, though I might avoid certain places or people sometimes because I’m worried about being watched.

Before these beliefs started, would you describe yourself as a generally suspicious or mistrustful person in relationships or with other people’s intentions, or does this level of suspicion feel very different from how you used to be?

Before all this started, I’d say I was a pretty normal level of cautious, but not especially suspicious or paranoid about people’s intentions. What I feel now is a lot more intense and constant than anything I remember experiencing before, so it does feel like a big change from my usual personality.

Have you ever felt that TV, radio, the internet, or other people could directly put thoughts into your mind, take thoughts out, or broadcast your thoughts so that others can hear them, or is it more that you feel watched and that messages are about you but your thoughts still feel private and under your own control?

It’s more that I feel watched and that things—like TV, online posts, or comments people make—are really about me or directed at me. My thoughts still feel private and under my own control; I don’t feel like anyone is putting thoughts in, taking them out, or broadcasting them.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [F22.0, F20.0]. The patient describes a nearly two‑year history of fixed persecutory and referential beliefs (being monitored, messages directed at them) that are not shared by their cultural group, with minimal or no insight and clear associated distress and some interpersonal/occupational impact. There is no history of prominent mood episodes, no substance trigger, and no evidence of hallucinations, thought interference, thought disorder, or negative symptoms. Functioning is largely preserved aside from behaviors driven by the delusional beliefs, and there is no marked deterioration in self‑care or social/occupational functioning outside the impact of the beliefs themselves. This pattern strongly favors a persistent delusional disorder over schizophrenia, which in ICD‑10 typically requires additional first‑rank symptoms (e.g., thought insertion, running commentary voices), or more pervasive functional decline. Given the absence of such features over a prolonged course, F20.0 has become unlikely, so the current candidate list is narrowed to [F22.0]. I will continue the interview to confirm there are no subtle psychotic or mood symptoms and to clarify any other contributing factors before making a final diagnosis.

opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you—thanks for coming in today. What has been bothering you lately that made you decide to come see me?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has had a single, well‑systematized delusional theme (being monitored, messages directed at them) for almost two years, with strong conviction and minimal insight, not shared by their cultural group. There are no hallucinations, thought interference, or formal thought disorder, no prominent or sustained mood episodes, and no significant negative symptoms or functional decline beyond circumscribed avoidance related to the delusional beliefs. Symptoms are not attributable to substances. This pattern is most consistent with persistent delusional disorder (F22.0). Schizophrenia (F20.0) was considered but ruled out due to absence of first‑rank psychotic symptoms, hallucinations, or marked deterioration in functioning.
